draft.title: Show, don't tell
card: Telling names the feeling outright. For example: "Sam was nervous."
Showing lets the reader work out the feeling from what a character does, what is around them and what they say. For example: "Sam wiped his palms and checked the clock."
Writers can show a feeling through actions, small details and dialogue, such as a shaky voice or a slammed door.
Showing draws the reader in, because they feel the emotion for themselves instead of being handed a label.
draft.remember: Let the reader find the feeling in what a character does, notices and says.

a.q: Which sentence shows a character's feeling instead of telling it?
opts: Lena bit her lip and kept glancing at the door
Lena felt very worried about the visitor
Lena was anxious as she waited for the visitor
Lena had a worried feeling about the visitor
a.why: The first sentence lets the reader work out the worry from what Lena does. The others name the feeling outright with words such as worried and anxious, so they are telling.
a.clue: Which sentence never names the feeling?

b.q: Kai is writing a story and wants to show that Mia is angry, without using the word angry. Which line does this best?
opts: Mia slammed the locker and snapped, "Don't talk to me."
Mia was furious that Kai had broken her pencil case
Mia felt a huge wave of rage about the pencil case
Mia was so cross and upset that she could hardly speak
b.why: The slammed locker and sharp words let the reader work out Mia's anger from action and dialogue. The other lines name the feeling with words such as furious, rage and cross, even when the word angry is avoided, so they tell.
b.clue: Look for a line where the reader works out the feeling from what Mia does and says.

a.best: Lena bit her lip and kept glancing at the door

b.best: Mia slammed the locker and snapped, "Don't talk to me."
